author: Guest
title: Editorial: No joke | Editorials | timesargus.com
text:
While Jimmy Kimmel may be what Americans are talking about (and there is some validity in any discussion about the First Amendment and whether Donald Trump can take a joke), there are matters at hand that are no joke.
In fact, they are anything but funny.
Medical professionals are reacting with alarm to Trump’s unproven statements about Tylenol, childhood vaccines, and autism.
Overnight, Trump gave members of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement a semblance of validation.
Supporters of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — many of them anti-vaccine activists and others who distrust the American health care system entirely — see Trump’s recent comments as a watershed moment.
“I think that for the ‘MAHA’ movement, this is like the dark clouds have finally parted and a single ray of sunshine is shining down,” Del Bigtree, Kennedy’s former communications director and founder of the advocacy group Informed Consent Action Network, told a reporter in an interview on Tuesday.
By amplifying the movement’s long-held concerns about vaccines and pharmaceutical products, Trump handed a major victory to a group that has been growing in influence since he tapped Kennedy to oversee the nation’s health services. It’s a coalition that is viewed as a potentially important voting bloc for Republicans, but had become impatient with what they saw as inaction by his administration.
It does not seem to matter that the information is inaccurate. In fact, more reasoned leaders are insisting that people listen to health care providers.
At a news conference on Monday, Trump claimed that pregnant women using acetaminophen, the painkiller known by the brand-name Tylenol, has contributed to the rise in autism cases in the U.S. in recent years. While some studies have suggested a potential correlation between the two, many others haven’t found that concern.
Experts say the research is inconclusive, and the increase is mainly due to better diagnoses and a new definition for the disorder that now includes mild cases on a spectrum. In addition, the Coalition of Autism Scientists said this week that acetaminophen use during pregnancy hadn’t increased in recent decades as autism rates have.
Trump offered his own advice, urging pregnant women to “fight like hell” to avoid taking the most commonly used drug in the country. His advice also went beyond the more nuanced Food and Drug Administration guidance released this week, which notes that the potential correlation is an area of ongoing debate and that acetaminophen is the only over-the-counter drug approved for treating fever during pregnancy.
Untreated fevers in pregnancy, particularly the first trimester, increase the risk for miscarriages, preterm birth, and other problems, according to the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.
Trump and Kennedy also directly addressed the parents of children with autism, saying their trepidation about vaccines had not been affirmed enough from the national stage. “I want to reassure the people in the autism community that we will be uncompromising and relentless in our search for answers,” Kennedy said.
Media watchers say appealing to maternal concerns about children’s health can be incredibly persuasive and has become a common strategy in the anti-vaccine movement.
At one point in the news conference, Trump told a story about a woman who used to work with him in Trump Tower and claimed her young son got a high fever after receiving a vaccine. The President then added he knew at least two other people who were “badly hurt” by vaccinations, but did not go into detail.
But an anecdote does not a statistic make. Fortunately, the vast majority of parents in the U.S. are keeping their children up-to-date with recommended childhood vaccines. But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says rates have been falling for the past five years.
Nationwide, the percentage of kindergartners receiving the most common childhood vaccines dropped well below 95% — the level needed to protect the community against an outbreak.
Playing fast and loose with health care feels tenuous. Even within his own party, Trump had lawmakers voicing unease and concern.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, of Louisiana, a gastroenterologist, noted: “HHS should release the new data that it has to support this claim. ... The preponderance of evidence shows that this is not the case. The concern is that women will be left with no options to manage pain in pregnancy. We must be compassionate to this problem.”
Republican Tennessee Sen. Richard Briggs, a cardiothoracic surgeon, cautioned individuals to check with their physicians about acetaminophen and vaccinations.
The President of the United States should not be making those kinds of pronouncement with no personal expertise, no scientific background, and no support of the experts. We are not even talking about ridiculous claims of ingesting bleach, horse pills, or shining light inside the human body to clear out COVID.
Mostly, Trump’s comments this week advanced a MAHA narrative discredited by decades of evidence that the ingredients in vaccines or taking immunizations close together can cause autism in children.
“We should all just be incredibly grateful,” MAHA Action President Tony Lyons said on Steve Bannon’s show this week, adding that Trump should be known as the “MAHA” president.
This kind of misinformation is nothing to laugh at. We’re sure the makers of Tylenol aren’t finding any humor in it.
